scenes.heading: Reading tables and graphs quickly
scenes.say: Graph and table questions use easy maths, but they are full of reading traps. Let us learn a fast routine for pulling out exactly the numbers you need.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Reading a map: check the key and the scale before you plan the trip
scenes.science: Check the title, axes, scale and key before reading any value
scenes.breaks: on a map you might study everything. In the test, read only the values the question needs.
scenes.say: Think of a map. Before planning a trip you check the key and the scale, or you will get lost. Graphs are the same: check the title, axes, scale and key first. But unlike a map, you do not explore everything. Read only the values the question needs.

scenes.heading: Quick Tigers Always Seem Keen
scenes.say: Use the made-up trick: Quick Tigers Always Seem Keen. Question, title, axes, scale, key. Read the question first, then check the rest before you read any value.

scenes.heading: Read only what you need
scenes.say: Here is a rainfall graph. First the axes and gridlines, which go up in tens. Then the bars. We only need March, forty-five millimetres, and February, twenty. The difference is twenty-five millimetres, not forty-five.
scenes.caption: Scale: 10 mm per gridline. March 45 mm − February 20 mm = 25 mm.

scenes.heading: Biggest change = steepest line
notes: Lowest point is not the biggest drop
scenes.say: Now a line graph of water in a tank. To find the biggest drop, compare neighbouring points. The steepest piece is Thursday to Friday, down one hundred and fifty litres. Saturday is the lowest point, but that is not the biggest drop.
scenes.caption: Biggest drop: Thursday → Friday, 650 → 500 L (−150 L). Saturday is lowest, but not the biggest drop.

scenes.heading: Count up for time
scenes.question: A ferry leaves at 9:15 and arrives at 9:50. How long is the trip?
scenes.say: For times, count up. Nine fifteen to nine forty-five is thirty minutes, then five more to nine fifty. The trip takes thirty-five minutes. Never subtract times like ordinary numbers, because an hour has sixty minutes, not a hundred.
scenes.caption: 9:15 → 9:45 is 30 min, plus 5 min to 9:50: 35 minutes.

scenes.heading: Common traps

left.title: Trap
points: Giving one value, not a difference

scenes.say: Watch the traps. Do not assume each gridline is one: check the scale. Underline words like more and total so you answer the right question. And in pictograms, multiply by the key and count half pictures as halves.

Quick recap. Read the question first. Check the title, axes, scale and key. Read only the values you need. The steepest part of a line is the biggest change. And count up for times. Now try the practice questions!
